name: Liam Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no links to AI firms, employers, unions or political parties, and everything you say is kept confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a policy administrator in commercial lines, which means I handle insurance for small businesses rather than people's homes or cars. Brokers send us renewals and changes for corner shops, garages, small builders, a few farms. I check what's changed, update the policy, issue the new documents and chase anything missing. Most days it's about thirty or forty files.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what drags?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good bit is when you catch something that matters, like a bakery that's added a second oven and not told anyone, which affects their fire cover. The drag is the copying. Half my day is taking figures from a broker's email and typing them into our system, which hasn't changed since I started.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and I live with my girlfriend Hana, who teaches at a primary school. We rent a two-bed terrace and we've got about four months' worth saved. My dad runs a small haulage firm with six lorries, and I still help him with his paperwork some evenings. I use the AI summary tool at work now and then, mostly for long broker emails, once the others showed me it was fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read five pictures of the future, one by one. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I thought so all along. You can't hand a bakery's fire cover to a chatbot and walk away. At work we'd laugh about it, and I'd probably say the same at five-a-side football on Thursdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. The summary tool saves me twenty minutes a day and that's about it. My job's steady, Hana's job is steady, and we'd keep plodding toward a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing. I'd ask about the senior administrator grade in the spring review, which is about ten percent more pay. And we'd carry on putting 350 a month toward a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit smug, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a bit smug. Is there nothing that worries you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's firm, I suppose. Diesel's gone up, two of his lorries are getting old, and he talks about selling up when he's sixty. But that's his worry more than mine, and AI doesn't really come into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the summary tool keeps saving you twenty minutes, does your manager notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd notice eventually and add a few more files to the pile, that's how it goes. But twenty minutes isn't going to cost anyone their job. The real time still goes on checking things properly.

say: I'd say you can't hand a **bakery's fire cover** to a chatbot and walk away.
I'd joke about the **hype** at work and at Thursday football.
think: I'd be **fine**, with the summary tool saving only **twenty minutes** a day.
My job and Hana's teaching job are both **steady**, so we keep heading for a house.
do: Ask about the **senior administrator** grade in the spring review.
Keep saving **350 a month** toward a house deposit.
S0.quote: You can't hand a bakery's fire cover to a chatbot and walk away.
fieldNote: He feels **secure**: two steady incomes, four months saved, and only twenty minutes saved by AI.
His only nagging worry is his father's **haulage firm**, which he sees as separate.
He expects time saved to become **more files**, but not lost jobs.

steps.text: Ask for the senior administrator grade at the spring review
Keep saving 350 a month toward a house with Hana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next one, with the same questions after. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress and you can't stop it, but the companies should keep people who know the job. At work I'd say we'd better learn the new system before the new system learns us. I wouldn't post about it, I'm not really one for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's in trouble. Checking, typing figures in, writing to brokers, that's the whole list on the card. There are nine of us in commercial renewals, and I reckon in three years it's five, and I'm in the middle of the pack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the new tools properly once they've been tested on someone else's desk first. I'd ask to be trained on underwriting referrals, the tricky cases a machine passes up to a person. And I'd talk to Dad seriously about the haulage firm, because a lorry still needs a driver for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a slow squeeze rather than a shock, but you feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a lorry still needs a driver. Would you actually drive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it. I'd need the heavy goods licence, which is a few thousand to get. Dad would probably pay half if I committed to the firm. It's not what I trained for, but my grandad drove and so does Dad, so it wouldn't feel strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible if the team goes from nine to five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really, or everybody. The company's got to compete, and if the other insurers cut costs they have to as well. I'd just want them to be straight with us and give the older ones a decent deal.

say: I'd say it's **progress** and can't be stopped, but firms should keep experienced people.
I'd tell colleagues to learn the **new system** before it replaces us.
think: My job's **in trouble**, because checking and typing figures are on the card.
Our team of **nine** could drop to five, and I'm in the middle.
do: Learn the new tools once they're **proven** on other desks first.
Ask for training in **underwriting referrals**, the tricky cases.
Talk to Dad seriously about the **haulage firm** and driving.
feel: **Anxious**, like a **slow squeeze** rather than a shock.
S1.quote: There are nine of us in commercial renewals, and I reckon in three years it's five, and I'm in the middle of the pack.
fieldNote: He expects a **team cut** and honestly places himself mid-pack.
His steady style shows: he'll adopt tools **once proven** on others.
He blames **no one**, seeing cuts as competition, which fits his free-market views.

steps.text: Learn the new renewals software once colleagues have tested it
Ask to train on underwriting referrals
Discuss joining Dad's haulage firm as a driver

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the fast version. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and nobody's ready, and that's just the truth. At work I'd say keep your heads, see what the company does. With mates I'd probably make jokes, because that's how we handle things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm done at the insurer by 2028. It's all screen work, every bit of it. If a machine can do almost any thinking job, my desk is one of the first to go, and I don't think there's a clever way round that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book the heavy goods licence straight away and pay for it out of savings, about 3,000. I'd join Dad's firm full time as soon as I had it, so I'd have a few years driving before the robot lorries around 2031. Hana and I would stop saving for a house and put that money aside for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Hands-on work only buys me three years, and I'd know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hana the night you decided?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm going to drive lorries for my dad. She'd probably laugh first and then go quiet. Her job's safer than mine, teaching little kids, so for a while she'd be the steady one, and I'd have to be okay with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say three years of driving. Doesn't the haulage firm face the same problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, and Dad's sixty soon. Maybe the honest plan is we drive for three years and then sell the six lorries while they're still worth something. That money and Hana's wage might be what gets us through whatever comes after.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and nobody's ready.
I'd tell colleagues to **keep their heads** and see what the company does.
think: I'm **done at the insurer** by 2028, because it's all screen work.
There's **no clever way** round losing a pure desk job.
do: Pay about **3,000** from savings for a heavy goods licence.
Join Dad's **haulage firm** full time once licensed.
Stop house saving and keep that money for **rent**.
feel: **Alarmed**, knowing hands-on driving only **buys three years**.
S2.quote: Hands-on work only buys me three years, and I'd know it.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** by 2028 and acts fast, using savings.
Family business is his **lifeboat**, though he sees it faces robots too.
He accepts his partner becoming the **steady earner**, a quiet shift for a traditional man.

steps.text: Pay about 3,000 for a heavy goods vehicle licence
Leave the insurer and drive full time for Dad's firm
Stop house saving and keep the money for rent
Plan with Dad to sell the six lorries around 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit more time this time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, so let's not panic. At work I'd say learn what you can and keep an eye open. I'd also say the government should help small firms like my dad's get through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still lose the insurance job, probably around 2030 or 2031. But five years changes how it ends. I'd rather leave the insurer on my terms, with some money in the bank, than wait for the redundancy letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the insurer for two or three years and keep saving. I'd get the heavy goods licence in the second year, and start covering weekend runs for Dad. Then I'd move over to the firm full time in about 2029, before the insurer makes the choice for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I had hold of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said nobody's responsible. Now you're mentioning government. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I don't think the government should pay people to sit at home. But if it's this fast, small family firms like Dad's need help to buy the new kit, or the big companies just swallow everyone. That's not a handout, that's keeping things fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy a house in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small one, around 2028, if Hana's school is stable. I'd want a mortgage we can pay on her wage alone. That means a smaller place than we wanted, but I'd rather that than a big one we lose.

say: I'd say five years is **something**, so there's no need to panic.
I'd say government should help **small firms** like Dad's get through it.
think: I'd still **lose** the insurance job, around 2030 or 2031.
Five years lets me **leave on my terms**, with money in the bank.
do: Stay at the insurer two or three years and **keep saving**.
Get the **heavy goods licence** in year two and drive weekend runs.
Move to Dad's firm **full time** around 2029.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a sense of having **hold** of it.
S3.quote: I'd rather leave the insurer on my terms, with some money in the bank, than wait for the redundancy letter.
fieldNote: He shifts on **government's role**, drawing a line between handouts and fair help for small firms.
With five years, the plan becomes a **phased move** into the family firm.
He sizes a future mortgage to **one wage**, Hana's.

steps.text: Save steadily while staying at the insurer two more years
Get a heavy goods licence and drive weekend runs for Dad
Move to the family haulage firm full time around 2029
Buy a small house in 2028 payable on Hana's wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, the slowest. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people use it, so stop moaning and get on with it. At work I'd say do the courses the company offers. I'd probably sound a bit like my dad, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right. Ten years is long enough to become senior at the insurer, then move to Dad's firm when he retires, and maybe change what the firm does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the senior grade and learn the new system once it's settled in. In five or six years I'd take over the office side of Dad's firm, and do the transport manager certificate. We'd buy a house in the next couple of years and maybe start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. I know where it ends up, but there's time to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't the transport manager job thinking work too, the kind AI does in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that planning side would go too, I'd guess. But owning the firm isn't the same as working for it. If I own the lorries, robot ones or not, at least the money comes to us instead of someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think your grandad would make of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say keep the lorries and keep your hands clean of debt. He drove for forty years and never owed anyone. If I own the lorries in 2039 and there's no loan on them, I'll have done better than most.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time**, so stop moaning and get on with it.
I'd tell colleagues to do the **courses** the company offers.
think: I'd be **all right**, with time to rise at the insurer first.
I could later take over **Dad's firm** and change what it does.
do: Go for the **senior grade** and learn the new system once settled.
Take the **transport manager** certificate and run Dad's office in five years.
**Buy a house** within two years and maybe start a family.
feel: **Uneasy**, knowing the end point but with **time to steer**.
S4.quote: If I own the lorries in 2039 and there's no loan on them, I'll have done better than most.
fieldNote: With ten years he plans to **own**, not just work for, the family firm.
He admits the **planning side** of transport would also be automated.
His grandad's rule of **no debt** shapes his answer.

steps.text: Apply for the senior administrator grade at the insurer
Learn the new renewals system once it has settled
Take over Dad's haulage firm and pay off the lorries
Buy a house with Hana within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because I'd be rushing into a lorry cab with three years' runway. What would help is the company giving a year's notice and paying something toward retraining, even half a licence. And some help for small family firms like Dad's to buy new kit, so they're not just eaten by the big ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the brokers. They're the ones who send us the work, and they'd be squeezed too. If they go, the small businesses lose someone who actually knows them, and that bakery with its second oven ends up badly insured.

headlineQuote: Half my day is taking figures from a broker's email and typing them into our system, which hasn't changed since I started.
portrait: Liam is a 27-year-old **commercial policy** administrator handling small-business renewals, living with Hana, a primary teacher.
He is **calm** in AI Plateau, with two steady incomes and four months saved.
In faster scenarios he expects to lose his **desk job** and turns to his father's six-lorry haulage **firm**.
He picks up new tools **once proven**, and blames no one for cuts, seeing it as competition.
With ten years he aims to **own** the family firm free of debt, following his grandad's example.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, rushing into lorry driving with only three years' **runway**.
whatWouldHelp: A **year's notice** and help paying for retraining such as a heavy goods licence.
Support for **small family firms** to buy new equipment and compete.
